Is Canada’s EU Courtship Realpolitik or Romance?
As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney prepares to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, a question once relegated to the realm of political fantasy is gaining traction in Ottawa and Brussels: Could Canada join the European Union? While full membership remains a legal labyrinth and a political long shot, the surge in dialogue signals a profound strategic realignment driven by transatlantic friction and a shared desire for democratic resilience.
The timing of Prime Minister Carney’s visit is no coincidence. Arriving in Strasbourg on September 16 to speak at the State of the European Union (SOTEU) address, Carney steps onto the stage at a moment when Europe is redefining its security architecture and Canada is seeking to diversify its geopolitical dependencies. Although EU membership is not officially on the agenda, the subtext of the visit is clear: Canada is seeking a deeper, more institutionalized bond with the bloc, potentially exploring models like "associate status" that go beyond traditional trade agreements.
The Legal Labyrinth: Can a Non-European Country Join?
The immediate hurdle to Canadian membership is Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, which states that any "European State" may apply to join. The definition of "European" is both geographic and political. While countries like Turkey and Cyprus have applied despite complex geographic realities, Canada’s location in North America presents a fundamental treaty barrier.
Amending the EU treaties to allow for non-European members would require unanimity among all 27 member states, a politically Herculean task. Furthermore, the EU’s current focus is on internal consolidation and the accession of Western Balkan nations, Ukraine, Moldova, and Georgia. Adding a G7 economy from another continent would require a complete overhaul of the EU’s institutional balance, budgetary contributions, and voting weights.
However, the concept of "associate status" offers a more feasible, albeit undefined, pathway. Unlike full membership, associate status could grant Canada participation in specific EU programs such as Horizon Europe for research, Galileo for satellite navigation, or even aspects of the single market for critical minerals without requiring adherence to the full acquis communautaire (the body of EU law). This model would allow for deep integration without the political toxicity of treaty change.
The Political Driver: Washington’s Unreliability
The primary catalyst for this rapprochement is not necessarily a love affair with Brussels, but a growing estrangement from Washington. Under the second term of President Donald Trump, the US-Canada relationship has been strained by aggressive tariff policies, demands for higher defense spending, and a transactional approach to alliances that unsettles Ottawa.
For Canada, the EU represents a stable, rules-based counterweight to American unpredictability. By deepening ties with Europe, Canada can reduce its economic overdependence on the US, which currently accounts for nearly 75% of its exports. For the EU, Canada is an attractive partner: a stable democracy, a rich source of critical minerals needed for the green transition, and a like-minded ally in the Indo-Pacific strategy.
The discussions around critical minerals are particularly significant. As the EU seeks to decouple its supply chains from China and Russia, Canada’s vast reserves of lithium, cobalt, and rare earths offer a secure alternative. A formalized partnership could see Canadian resources integrated into European battery and tech manufacturing, creating a transatlantic industrial base that is resilient to external shocks.
Beyond Trade: Security and Values
The upcoming talks are expected to cover joint high-tech and security-infrastructure projects, reflecting a shift from purely economic cooperation to strategic alignment. With Europe ramping up its defense capabilities in response to Russian aggression, Canada’s involvement in NATO and its technological prowess in AI and cybersecurity make it a valuable partner.
Moreover, both Ottawa and Brussels are grappling with the rise of authoritarianism and the erosion of democratic norms globally. A closer alliance would signal a commitment to defending liberal democratic values, from press freedom to judicial independence, in an increasingly multipolar world.
A Temporary Flirtation or a New Era?
Skeptics argue that this surge in interest is a temporary response to tensions with Washington, likely to fade if US-Canada relations improve under a different administration. However, the structural shifts in the global economy and security landscape suggest otherwise. The era of unquestioned American hegemony is giving way to a more fragmented world where middle powers like Canada must cultivate multiple strong partnerships.
While full EU membership remains a legal and political fantasy for now, the exploration of associate status and deeper integration is a serious strategic move. It reflects a recognition that Canada’s future security and prosperity are inextricably linked to Europe’s stability and success.
As Mark Carney takes the podium in Strasbourg, he will not be asking for a seat at the table of EU ministers. But he will be laying the groundwork for a new kind of table, one where Canada and Europe sit as equal partners, bound not just by trade, but by shared values, security interests, and a common vision for a resilient democratic order. Whether this leads to a formal union or just a stronger friendship, the message is clear: the North Atlantic bridge is being rebuilt, and this time, it’s being strengthened against the storms ahead.

Signs to Come
Nathan I drove up from a wedding the day of the date. I arrived in time to shower and take the train down. I met a friend and we walked to the spot together, at which point I kindly told him to go find something else to do.
Claire I got ready with my roommates.
Nathan My first impression was, Wow, this girl is short! (She is 5 foot 2.) And then, Woah, she’s dressed kind of badass, because she was rocking a black leather jacket.
Claire He’s very tall! He’s handsome too, and has nice hair.
Higher Power
Nathan We talked about our jobs and where we’re hoping to go in our lives. Turns out, we’re both considering becoming social workers. I was genuinely riveted when she told me her horror stories from summer camp. She also told me she doesn’t listen to music on her commute because she likes to use that time to daydream. I thought that was one of the most interesting things I’d ever been told.
Claire I learned that he was taking a break from divinity school, and that he had been researching substance-use disorders through a spiritual lens. My work relates to mental health, so I was immediately interested in learning more. We spoke about what inspired him to study religion in undergrad and talked about the different religions he learned about. Also, he told me he was in a band, and plays the bass.
Nathan We ordered some grilled zucchini and a large crab cake, and a round of oysters. Later, we got the tuna carpaccio.
Claire The carpaccio was the standout. We also had some champagne and then I tried the Northern Lights cocktail, which was also delicious.
Nathan This first date was noticeably more comfortable than others I’ve been on. We began to tease each other more and care less about what exactly was being talked about.
Claire He’s very easy to talk to. On the way out I grabbed his arm, and we ended up holding hands. It was sweet.
Open Minds
Nathan I was excited to continue the date, so while she washed up I chitchatted with the staff to assess our options.
Claire After dinner, Nathan suggested two bars nearby. I was happy to continue the evening, so we headed to one.
Nathan The date ended with me walking her home. We were pretty happy in each other’s company on the walk back, it seemed to me; I went to give her a little spin at the end of the date and she misinterpreted it, fairly, I think, as a handshake. I was hoping we might feel a little chemistry in that moment, but it didn’t really work out — which is OK!
Claire He offered to walk me home, which I thought was nice. We stood at the corner and chatted for a bit longer, and then we hugged and parted ways.
Second Date?
Nathan I think we will! We have begun chitchatting about it.
Claire I would! I don’t see us running out of conversation topics anytime soon.
Grading the Date
Nathan / B+
Claire / A

When we dropped by on the sets of Maddy, Rio and Saniya Iyappan were shooting at a cricket stadium. The atmosphere on set was young, fun and relaxed. The cast and crew proceeded to speak to us about the film, which revolves around a man and woman who are complete opposites.
It's a jolly, fun-loving story. My character, Sachin, studies in a boys' school and concentrates on sports, as his dad (played by Singampuli) wants him to become a cricketer. As a result, he is hesitant to speak to girls. How he finds and interacts with his lover is what the story is about. Although my character’s name is Sachin, Maddy is the name he gives himself. Saniya plays a strong character in the film, which has provided us both equal screen space and performance scope
-Rio, actor
This character is different from the other roles I did in Tamil. It's closer to the real me… someone who travels and is bubbly and modern. I play an influencer. Every heroine has the dream to have a special entry or slo-mo frames for them. In Maddy, you can see me in a proper heroine vibe. When I heard Rio was doing the film, I said, 'I'm in,' because he is an amazing actor whom I like a lot. It's been a fun set. There are nice songs in the film. As a dancer, you wish to dance to good songs, and I got the opportunity in Maddy.
Aju chettan and I haven't worked together in Malayalam. This is our first film together.
-Saniya Iyappan, actress
Rio is a very close friend of mine. I'm happy that I get to play his friend in the film as well. Aju (Varghese) bro is super sweet. BK bro is a young new-generation director. When a team of youngsters come together and begin a startup, there will be a certain kind of energy. That's also the case with this film. Maddy is very close to our heart.
-Vijay, actor
It's a cricket-based love story. It's about what happens when two extremely opposite characters, who are also cricket fans, meet. Basically, it's about a friendly girl and a guy who doesn't know how to speak with girls. Today, the shoot is at a stadium. The heroine is from Bengaluru and is an influencer. Saniya is always on time, and it's been superb working with her. I'm a big Aju Varghese fan. I wrote the role for Yogi Babu, but there was an issue with his dates. I like Aju Varghese sir as much as Yogi Babu, so when we approached him, he also sweetly agreed.
- Karthikeyan BK, director
Maddy is Rio’s biggest film in terms of casting and scale. There's a cricket connection in the film that plays an important factor between the lead characters It's a love story that will connect with boys today with a cricketing and dating app angle. The director wanted Aju, as he felt it would be fresh and unique. I've followed Saniya’s work, and she is the apt choice for the role.

The trouble with dating apps is that the carousel never stops. How can anyone make a considered decision about Daisy from Putney when Julia from Richmond is a thumb-twitch away? And somewhere behind Julia, surely, is someone even better. After years of swiping, the patient zero of our interminable romantic misery, the apps, are finally in their death rattle. If they achieved one thing, it’s uniting the world against them.
With the apps came dating insanity. I’ve had my fair share. One match popped up with a gallery of elegant, charismatic photos and a profile Jane Austen could have written. She turned out not to be in her late thirties, as the beautiful prose suggested, but in her mid to late seventies. How did she get away with it? Simple. She’d used her daughter’s photos because, in her words: “I get more matches that way.”
Can’t argue with that. Over the froth of my seemingly never-ending cappuccino, I asked: “But… does it work?” “Oh yes,” she said. “I’ve had loads of fun with younger men.” To be fair to her, the sex was fantastic (kidding). And she wasn’t even the strangest. There was the beautiful woman who took me back to her Surrey mansion, where her husband was waiting in the hallway, in a leather armchair, naked from the waist down.
Apps are a dopamine drip that never runs dry but they don’t actually work because romance was never going to be found by searching. It grows out of attraction and chemistry, one of the few parts of being human that still feels like magic.
I’m not alone in retiring my exhausted digits. In a single year, Tinder, Hinge and Bumble lost more than a million UK users between them. And the people my age who hang on are the most devoted of all. 55- to 64-year-olds on dating apps spend nearly six hours on them in a month, longer than any other age group. That’s a lot of evenings scrolling past partners in crime.
And it’s mostly men doing the swiping: more than six in 10 people using dating services in the UK are male, which will surprise no woman with thumbs. What men get wrong is written all over their profiles. In my work helping people in acute emotional pain, break-up and divorce, I hear from women who are on the apps even in their heartbreak. The relentless draw of the next swipe keeps them chasing the dating app dragon, and they end up drowning in a sea of clichés. If men say they want “no drama, no time-wasters”, they are talking about their last relationship, not hopes for the next one.
Apps are having to adapt too. Tinder has introduced an “events” tab where users can choose to go on real-life dates, from trivia nights to ceramics classes. So, the company that invented “the swipe”, now wants you in a room with other people, making a wonky mug.
These days I give relationship advice to more than 400,000 women on social media. I’ve heard it all: the ghosting, the man who messaged for three weeks and never once suggested a coffee, the profile photos with the ex badly cropped out. I’ve built a whole part of my business offering advice on meeting people in real life.
So, if you’re ready to put the phone down, here’s where I’d start.
Go somewhere more than once. A weekly class, a choir, a walking group, a volunteering shift. The first week you’re a stranger. By the fourth, you’re a familiar face. Attraction often grows out of simply seeing someone regularly.
Choose things you would enjoy even if you met nobody. If the only point of the evening is finding someone, every evening without them is a failure. If you’d happily go anyway, you’re relaxed and better company. Nobody has ever been charmed by someone gritting their teeth through salsa.
Take a friend, then talk to other people. Arriving with someone makes walking through the door easier. Just make a rule before you go in, so you don’t spend the whole evening talking only to each other.
Say yes to the invitations you’d normally dodge. The 50th birthday, the leaving drinks, the barbecue at the house of a friend of a friend. An awful lot of good relationships still start with someone saying: “You must meet my friend.”
If you do stay on the apps, put them in their place. Set a time limit, check them at set times rather than all evening and move to meeting in person quickly. A week of messaging tells you far less than 20 minutes over a coffee.
The swipe had a good run. But it made us fussy, and a little greedy, always sure someone better was one flick away. My seventysomething coffee date understood the game better than any of us: the apps reward the picture, and she’d simply borrowed a better one. The rest of us might do better turning up, again and again, until someone notices.
Harry Hardisty writes about relationships, heartbreak and mid-life at dadhugsforyoursoul.com

It’s no secret that everyone is a little tired of dating apps. In 2024, research showed that consistent users of these apps were experiencing burnout symptoms. If you’ve ever spent 30 minutes swiping left on a sea of cringe prompt responses and pictures of men holding fish, you’re not surprised at this. Conversations seem to go nowhere, people feel very brave saying unhinged things to each other through a screen, and everyone is lying about their height.
Throwing in a subscription fee on top of that? No.
We get it: Businesses need to make money. But when a dating app hides its best features—you know, the ones that actually help you get a date—behind a paywall, it makes a user a lot less likely to want to keep swiping.
And while plenty of apps have jumped on this capitalistic train of “selling” love, not all of them have left their users with the scraps of the apps.
There are still some dating apps that are letting users look for love without having to plug in their credit card information. So you’re free (literally) to focus on what’s important: finding someone you think you could tolerate enough to go on a date with IRL.
Facebook Dating
Okay, the idea of still being on Facebook is daunting enough, so I understand the hesitation of dating on it. But as someone who has tried Facebook Dating in the past, I have to say it’s actually a pretty good dating platform. And if you’re worried that it’s just a means of dating people you “friended” in high school, it’s not.
It has a free matching and messaging experience, and if you already have Facebook downloaded you don’t have to worry about adding another app to your phone.
Feeld
If you’re looking for a dating experience outside of the norms of modern-day courting, Feeld is a great (and free) option. It’s for people looking to explore everything from nonmonogamy to casual hookups and other relationship styles. You can create a profile, connect with mutual likes, and chat—all without paying. While there are tiers that require a subscription, those just come with unlimited likes and the option to see who liked you.
Hinge
Okay, Hinge is definitely an app that has some features locked behind a payment but the app still offers a lot of great options for people who don’t want to whip out their credit card. The free version of the app gives you all of the essentials: browsing profiles, sending likes, matching, and chatting with matches. Just keep in mind that there’s a daily like limit (but I’ve never reached it, so you’ll be fine).
Tinder
Tinder is probably going to give you the biggest possible dating pool—and a lot of that access is for free. You can create a profile, like people, match, and message for free. The only thing to note is that using the paid option will give you access to premium prompts and the ability to set certain preferences.
Bumble
All of Bumble’s basic features (including its safety verification ones) are totally free when you download the app. This means you can find matches and—if you identify as a woman—message first all for free. The app lets you have safe, meaningful interactions without having to pay a dime.
OkCupid
If you want more than three photos and some prompts to base your swipe on, OkCupid is a great option. It’s free tier includes compatibility-focused profiles and extensive questions so you’re really getting a good idea of who someone is before you match with them.

Senate clears Blackburn-backed bill requiring dating app fraud alerts
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WZTV) — The U.S. Senate has passed a bipartisan bill backed by Tennessee Sen. Marsha Blackburn that would require dating apps to alert some users when an account that messaged them is banned for suspected financial fraud.
The Senate passed H.R. 2481, known as the Romance Scam Prevention Act, without amendment by unanimous consent on Sept. 23. The House passed the measure in June 2025, meaning the bill now heads to President Donald Trump.
Blackburn, a Republican, introduced Senate companion legislation with Democratic Sen. John Hickenlooper of Colorado. The measure that cleared Congress was introduced in the House by Republican Rep. David Valadao of California.
If signed, the law would take effect one year after enactment.
Under the bill, an online dating service would have to send a fraud-ban notification to a user who received a message from an account that was later banned because the service determined there was a significant risk the account holder would try to fraudulently obtain money.
MORE NEWS | New Tennessee poll shows Blackburn with big lead, Trump's approval underwater
The requirement would not apply to every person who may have interacted with the account. The bill specifically refers to users who received a message from the banned account through the dating service.
The notice would need to identify the banned account and tell the recipient when they most recently sent or received a message with that user. It also would need to warn that the person may have used a false identity or attempted to defraud users, advise people not to send cash or financial information and provide fraud-prevention resources and customer-service contact information.
Dating apps generally would have 24 hours after issuing a fraud ban to send the notice. The bill allows an app to take up to three days in some circumstances and permits longer delays if requested by law enforcement during an active investigation.
RELATED COVERAGE | Man accused of posing as 49ers player in $1.3M romance scam seen in video
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the law, while state attorneys general and other authorized state consumer-protection officials could bring civil actions.
The legislation focuses on a common way romance scammers try to build trust before seeking money. The FTC reported that nearly 70,000 people reported romance scams in 2022, with reported losses reaching $1.3 billion.
But dating apps are only one route scammers use. Among 2022 romance-scam loss reports that identified a contact method, the FTC said 40% began on social media and 19% began on a website or app.
In Tennessee, the FBI reported that people 60 and older filed 1,577 fraud complaints in 2023 and reported losing about $43.75 million. That was up from about $36.57 million in reported losses in 2022 — an increase of roughly 19.6%.
Those Tennessee figures include all reported fraud types involving people 60 and older, not romance scams alone.
The FTC advises people not to send cash, gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency to someone they know only online. Suspicious profiles or messages can be reported to the dating app and to ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

item.content:encoded:
Matchmaking is having a moment, whether it's an AI matchmaker for college students or human matchmakers with decades of experience. And while singles are increasingly vexed by dating apps, the platforms are trying to pull in loved ones to help them date, too — like with Hinge's recent feature Friend's Take.
Amid these trends, a new app for both singles and wannabe matchmakers launches today: Rivet. Founded by former Tinder and Match Group executive Taru Kapoor, Rivet is a "social matching" app that will attempt to replace algorithms with the wisdom of crowds. Users sign up as Daters or Matchers, and all are encouraged to pair up others.
"Dating has always been social," said Kapoor in a press release shared with Mashable. She spent years thinking that dating apps were removing friction from meeting each other, but instead, "we removed the people."
You May Also Like
AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections
Tinder — top pick for finding hookups
Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups
Dating apps created matches by connecting people who wouldn't have met otherwise, Kapoor continued, but a side effect was that they turned something fundamentally social and human — dating — into a transactional, isolated activity.
"I built Rivet to change that," she said. "Rivet is built on a simple truth: humans understand chemistry and compatibility in a way that no algorithm can. You don't have to find your person entirely on your own, let people help you find your person."
How does Rivet work?
On Rivet, all Daters are also Matchers, but not all Matchers are Daters, Kapoor told Mashable. "Even if you're married, in a relationship or simply not currently looking to date, you can still join Rivet to be a Matcher and help people find meaningful connections," she said over email. You can make a Dater profile later if you'd like, but you're never required to.
Matchers provide their opinions on potential pairs and recommend introductions for users they believe would be a good couple. Pairs who receive high "Social Matching scores" are then introduced to each other on the app, and each person decides whether to match and start a conversation.
You can be on Rivet solely as a Dater, Kapoor continued, though the app encourages Daters to participate in matching others.
More than two-thirds (68 percent) of Gen Z and millennials said they'd be interested in helping someone they don't personally know find a potential romantic match (if they can do so anonymously, and the pair themselves made the final decision), according to a national survey of over 2,000 U.S. adults commissioned by Rivet.
And some prizes can sweeten the deal, too. Matchers can receive rewards for helping people find love, according to Rivet's website. "Match a pair that you think will click or call a mismatch, and you earn Karma. Karma gets you bragging rights and can be redeemed for rewards," it states.
Currently, reaching 15,000 Karma with a strong MQ (Matcher Quotient, the app's way of displaying a Matcher's thoughtfulness and accuracy) can be redeemed for $30 equivalent in cash or gift cards, Kapoor said. The team is working on making more reward and redemption options available soon.
Those with high MQ might also be bestowed as Elite Matchers.
In addition to the app, Rivet also hosts live events, such as a dating show in New York City in early Oct.
More dating apps are adding AI — meaning, more algorithms — and Rivet is bucking the trend. It's now available for free on iOS and Android.
Anna Iovine is the associate editor of features at Mashable. Previously, as the sex and relationships reporter, she covered topics ranging from dating apps to pelvic pain. Before Mashable, Anna was a social editor at VICE and freelanced for publications such as Slate and the Columbia Journalism Review. Follow her on Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
The dating world is so bleak right now that some singles are calling restaurants/bars ahead of time to see whether any cute guys are there. And while this is a harmless, silly dating trend, it shows how much daters crave actual meet-cutes. Surely, they can just swipe on an app and find a dinner date that way. But there’s something special about meeting someone out in the real world. You know, the old-fashioned way.
In fact, according to Hily Dating App data, 62% of Gen Z women and 55% of Gen Z men are open to meeting someone IRL. The problem? Well, 38% of women and 42% of men also feel anxious about approaching strangers. Perhaps that is why some call ahead of time, mentally preparing for the dating pool they’re about to dip their toes into for the evening.
Videos by VICE
What Does the Calling-Ahead Trend Reveal About Modern Dating?
According to Dr. Sabrina Romanoff, a relationship expert at Hily Dating App and Harvard-trained clinical psychologist, this trend highlights the tension in modern dating.
“It’s ironic that people are trying to manufacture these impromptu and spontaneous meet-ups while simultaneously trying to control variables like you can with online dating,” says Dr. Sabrina Romanoff. “It speaks to our current desire to have our cake and eat it too.”
Is the Calling-Ahead Trend Actually Beneficial?
Sure, this lighthearted, funny trend could help in dating, as it lets you analyze your options before you even see them. However, if you go into every social outing with the hope to meet someone, you’re likely missing out on genuine connections and chance encounters. Instead of constantly focusing on finding a partner, try being present in every moment, whether grabbing drinks with your friends or having dinner with family.
“I would not recommend this approach because it comes with the mindset that going out, spending time with your girlfriends, and having new experiences are only ‘successful’ if you meet a cute potential new partner,” says Dr. Romanoff. “This inevitably places pressure on dating—it can make you feel more desperate and often leave you feeling worse if you don’t achieve your ‘objective’ at the end of the night.”
Trust me, I know how frustrating it can be to hear the advice of, “Just let love come to you!!!” and “It’ll happen when you least expect it!!!!” So, I won’t tell you either of those statements. They didn’t help me when I was single throughout my 20s, and honestly, they didn’t even prove to be true in my case. I had to actively work on myself and focus on my dating goals to find the right person.
But going to the other extreme of constantly dwelling on your singlehood and obsessing over meeting the love of your life won’t help either. So, sure, if you want to engage in this silly trend of calling a restaurant or bar ahead of time to scope out its patrons, go for it. Just don’t make meeting your person the core goal of every night out.

item.content:encoded:
- Published
The food distribution charity Felix spent £5.6m last year collecting surplus produce, and getting it to the community organisations it supports.
Richard Smith, director of food innovation at Felix, said: "These are costs we cannot cut. Without our logistics, this food would never reach the millions who need it most."
But a new platform dubbed "speed dating for trucks" has been launched to reduce those costs.
Using AI technology to bring together logistics providers, retailers and manufacturers, it matches spare haulage capacity with surplus food collections.
Early trials of the new software and system have already saved the charity money.
Smith added: "The benefits are all there - real and instant."
Deliveries of surplus food arrive all day at the Felix depot and kitchen in Poplar, east London.
It is sorted in the warehouse and redistributed to charities across London working to ease food poverty.
Until now, the administration has fallen to the logistics team at Felix (formerly the Felix Project), which books a haulier and pays for the transportation.
The costs soon add up.
Nicola Robinson, director of Alliance Food Sourcing (AFS) - a coalition of leading food companies - said: "Felix spent in 2025, £5.6m on 80,000 pallets, and three quarters of that cost was coming from third-party logistics companies.
"We thought we could take a look at that and if we tap into the spare capacity that we know exists within UK road hauliers, then we could put that to good use."
According to the Department for Transport, about 30% of all HGV journeys have spare capacity.
Using AI technology, the platform matches that space in lorries with deliveries to the Felix depots - hence the speed dating nickname.
Early trials with the food producer Greencore have led to a twice-weekly delivery of milk going to the Felix depot.
That route alone is projected to save the charity £20,000 a year.
Smith said: "The milk comes in every single week with very light touch from Felix, so we're barely getting involved.
"Now this is just a locked-in route, it happens every single week - that milk lands here and is back out to charities within 24 hours."
Currently, Greencore offers the service free of charge.
Darren Binns, head of logistics at Greencore, said: "There is an element of cost here but we think that we can absorb that cost, use the extra space that we have to do the right thing, to move surplus food into Felix's charity network."
Sainsbury's and logistics provider GXO have identified a further 10 routes for moving Felix food, with estimated annual savings of around £170,000.
Tesco, M&S and supply chain company Gist are also involved in the project, offering free consultancy and logistics support.
Data from the Trust for London showed that food insecurity has risen by 23% in London over the past two years.
Alongside the rise in need, transportation costs have gone up, and this is at a time when our changing climate sees demands that we reduce carbon emissions.
If the new platform is upscaled, AFS said it could save Felix £1m a year, as well as reduce road miles.
It said it would transform the way different sectors work, and urged more in the food industry to support the project.

item.content:encoded:
One of the worst sentences a girl’s friend group can hear is, “I downloaded Hinge again.” Generally, this can be excused following a breakup, but at its worst, it’s a woman defying her own logic and reasoning while crafting excuses for her horrible situationship “Because obviously, he’s super busy and nobody else understands.”
Despite arguments that having a boyfriend is currently a social faux pas, people still seek connection. Additionally, straight women’s dating frustrations have generated numerous pop albums, and even their own term, heterofatalism. Heterofatalism, coined by Asa Seresin, a sexuality scholar, describes the phenomenon of straight women feeling embarrassed about their attraction toward men and desire to detach themselves from the world of dating and subsequent disappointment.
I don’t think the issue here is that men simply suck. Nor do I think the death of chivalry is entirely to blame. Dating apps may be part of the problem. With a large selection of profiles, dating app users are more likely to reject the profiles accessible to them. Women experiencing this rejection mindset are less likely to obtain matches. Despite access to more potential partners on dating apps, the act of choosing the right partner isn’t as clear.
Sam Kizer, assistant professor of instruction in sociology at Ohio University, recognizes the influence of assistive technology in modern dating. He discussed the various dating resources marketed towards single people, including cards to bring to a date encouraging face-to-face conversations, dating apps and generative artificial intelligence.
“The algorithm, the tech, the dating, the cards, the apps, the cards, whatever, they might be able to assist in finding people to evaluate,” Kizer said. “They themselves cannot be the evaluator.”
Although dating apps create an opportunity to meet new people and potentially introduce users to new labels or types of relationships, the mere act of creating a profile requires the user to exclude potential matches to some degree. On Hinge, if you say you’re looking for a long-term relationship, the algorithm within the app is already curating who is and isn’t available for you as a potential match.
Alongside dating app usage, increased AI use in daily life, from email writing to LinkedIn job searches, hinders their ability to make independent critical decisions. Effective communication skills are vital to healthy relationships; this becomes an issue with a growing number of people using generative AI chatbots to analyze and support their relationship decisions.
Generation Z has faced numerous barriers to healthy social development, leading to an increase in social anxiety and loneliness. Utilizing online spaces to meet people can mitigate potential fear of rejection, but these online connections are not likely to help people feel less lonely.
Dating is meant to feel good, and it’s not surprising even pop music artists are calling out when it doesn't. Human connection is messy, vulnerable and cannot be calculated by an app or algorithm. Even if you or your best friend resorts to redownloading dating apps once again, try to remember taking a risk against your typical standards or expectations might not be so risky.
Alexa Sanders is a senior studying psychology at Ohio University. Please note the opinions expressed in this column do not represent those of The Post. Want to talk to Alexa about her column? Email her at al683822@ohio.edu.

item.content:encoded:
The rising cost of living has impacted singles for years now, and a new report from payment service Zelle shares new insights on just how much their bank accounts influence how (and if) they find love.
Zelle's Economics of Dating Report found that the vast majority (84 percent) of Gen Z and millennial daters say rising cost has affected their dating lives (according to an Aug. 2026 national survey of 1,800 Gen Z and millennial adults who've dated within the past year).
Around a third (32 percent) said they're going on fewer dates, and one in 10 (11 percent) have stopped dating because they can't afford it.
You May Also Like
AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections
Tinder — top pick for finding hookups
Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups
As Mashable reported this year, socioeconomic factors can definitely hinder dating. Not only can some young people not afford dates, but more are living at home and can't buy a home. This can then delay when people get married and have children.
But for those young adults still in the dating pool, Zelle's report found that some respondents are choosing less expensive activities (40 percent), preferring more frequent economical dates to occasional expensive ones (38 percent), and suggesting free activities (37 percent).
And in this economy, being seen as frugal is a good thing. Thirty-eight percent said they judged someone positively for planning an affordable, thoughtful date — more than the 23 percent who said the same for someone who put together an extravagant, high-end one.
Other financial green flags include being thoughtful with money (56 percent), being honest and transparent about money (54 percent), planning a thoughtful, budget-friendly date (52 percent), and paying without making the situation awkward (52 percent).
On the flipside, there are some red flags when it comes to money and dating, such as making someone uncomfortable about what they can afford, expecting the other person to pay for everything, complaining about every price, and talking too much about income — all of which 47 percent of participants said gave them the ick. Around the same amount, 46 percent, also flagged making a big deal about paying.
Money anxiety abounds these days, including when trying to find a partner. Among women respondents, being rejected and spending too much ranked equally as sources of dating anxiety (37 percent). Other sources of anxiety are spending too much on a date (34 percent of participants said this), making sure a date fits within their budget (29 percent), discussing finances (28 percent), and asking who pays (25 percent).
Twenty-six percent said they won't bring up payment with their date at all.
This all seems like glum news, but at least 89 percent of daters are still putting themselves out there. There are dating apps you can use for free and low-cost outings, too, like a walk in the park. Otherwise, some singles might find themselves turning to AI for a cheaper date.
Anna Iovine is the associate editor of features at Mashable. Previously, as the sex and relationships reporter, she covered topics ranging from dating apps to pelvic pain. Before Mashable, Anna was a social editor at VICE and freelanced for publications such as Slate and the Columbia Journalism Review. Follow her on Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
Dating apps don’t exactly have the best rep right now. Apps have seen a drop in users and just this month TIME declared that they are dead.
Everyone has their own guess as to why swiping feels slightly cringe: People want to make in-person connections, they think everyone on the apps is ugly, and, importantly users—mostly women—just don’t feel safe.
While I am a dating app retiree, I still vividly remember the amount of unhinged and frankly, frightening messages I received from men while on the apps. I know girlfriends who have been catfished, threatened, and even borderline stalked by men they swiped right on (and even ones they didn’t).
The people behind the apps are aware of the safety concerns and some (not all) have taken real steps to make sure their users feel as comfortable as possible—because trying to find love online is already difficult enough without having to worry about some creep using AI photos to trick you into meeting up.
So if you’re looking to swipe without worrying about your safety, here are some of the safest dating apps out there. Unfortunately, you’re on your own when it comes to what your matches look like.
Bumble
Despite the fact that I would never message a man first, Bumble is really steps ahead of a lot of other dating apps. They have one of the most extensive set of user-facing safety tools out there: photo verification, optional ID verification, and in-app voice and video calls. It also has the Share Date feature, which lets you share the details of an upcoming date with a trusted friend or family member. Plus, it blurs out potentially explicit photos, allows you to block, report, and unmatch someone, and even has a Deception Detector for users that are flagged as potential fake or scam accounts. It really gives you a lot of ways to vet someone before ever handing over your number.
Tinder
Tinder’s reputation has come a long way. What used to be known as “the hookup app” is now a pretty decent place to get to know someone—all while staying safe.
The app requires a Face Check, photo verification, Share My Date (similar to Bumble), and of course the ability to block and report someone. What really makes it a great option is the fact that users are prompted with “Are You Sure?” and “Does This Bother You?” message interventions to prompt people to think before they send something inappropriate, as well as the chance to report if something crosses the line.
Hinge
Hinge has become a lot more aggressive lately when it comes to authenticating its users. Its Face Check includes a video selfie and liveness check, which is then compared to profile photos. This can help detect duplicate or scam accounts.
Hinge’s Help Center also includes a variety of articles on “Safe Dating,” including pieces on consent, boundaries, and how to protect yourself from scammers.
Coffee Meets Bagel
Coffee Meet Bagel has always been known as a dating app for people who are really intentional about dating. And now, it has a bunch of safety features to make that more possible. The app has a live selfie verification—which has been completed by 70 percent of its users.
Match
Match focuses on moderation and user safety. Like some of the other apps on this list, it offers blocking, human moderation, anti-harassment measures, and privacy controls that lets users set who can contact them and what info goes on their profile. The app also gives users the chance to flag specifically for fake profiles, requests for money, and other violations.

item.content:encoded:
A recent study suggests that a woman’s level of religious belief influences how she evaluates potential partners on swipe-based dating apps like Tinder. When navigating these platforms, women often face a trade-off between evaluating a potential partner’s genetic fitness and their willingness to invest in a relationship. The findings indicate that more religious women show a broader initial receptivity to men’s profiles, while overall, women tend to prefer softer facial features but surprisingly favor exaggerated, unverifiable profile biographies. The research was published in Psychology & Sexuality.
Swipe-based dating applications require users to make split-second decisions about potential partners based on a single photograph and a brief biography. These platforms compress mate selection into rapid, low-consequence choices, forcing users to rely heavily on highly visible cues. When evaluating a photograph, people often pick up on facial sexual dimorphism, which refers to how physically masculinized or feminized a face appears.
Earlier research discovered that women often prefer softer, feminized male faces over hyper-masculine ones. For instance, a 1998 study showed that women routinely find feminized male faces more attractive than strictly masculine alternatives. This preference exists partly because rugged features are linked to lower trustworthiness, with a 2012 study indicating that women view more masculine men as more likely to engage in unfaithful behavior.
Religious norms often emphasize long-term relational stability and sexual restraint. Supporting this, a study covered by PsyPost in 2017 indicated that higher religious commitment is associated with a greater preference for long-term mating strategies and fewer sexual partners. Because of this association, researchers expected that religious women might be more cautious when evaluating potential partners online.
The new study builds on this concept by examining how initial visual judgments interact with written profile details and a woman’s own religiosity on modern dating apps. The research was conducted by Katherine L. Sheetz, a Ph.D. candidate, and Lisa L. M. Welling, a professor of psychology, both at Oakland University.
“Online dating has changed the way people make initial judgments about potential partners, especially since the COVID-19 pandemic forced the majority of dating online,” Welling, who directs the Welling Research Lab, told PsyPost. “Swipe-based platforms reduce initial mate choice selections to very rapid decisions based on relatively limited visual and textual information, yet we know relatively little about how individual differences, such as religiosity, shape those early decisions.”
“With this study, we were particularly interested in religiosity because it is associated with sexual restraint, restricted sociosexuality (meaning lower openness to casual sex), and long-term relationship motivations on average,” Welling explained. “We therefore wanted to test whether more religious women would be more selective when evaluating potential male partners in an online context, particularly when profiles contained cues that could be relevant to apparent trustworthiness and relationship intentions.”
The study included 439 single cisgender women between the ages of 18 and 38 who were primarily attracted to men. The participants completed an online survey that began with questionnaires assessing their religious beliefs and their motivations for using dating applications. Afterward, they completed a simulated Tinder task where they viewed 20 distinct male dating profiles. Each profile featured a photograph of a smiling man and a short, 500-character biography.
The researchers manipulated the photographs using computer software so that the faces appeared either 50 percent more masculinized or 50 percent more feminized, while keeping skin tone and identity the same. The profile biographies were also written to be either trustworthy or untrustworthy.
Trustworthy biographies included verifiable, specific information regarding education or employment and avoided grand claims. Untrustworthy biographies featured exaggerated personal achievements and vague job descriptions, a tactic known as selective self-presentation. The participants had to either accept each profile, mimicking a right swipe, or reject the profile, mimicking a left swipe.
The researchers found that facial features strongly guided the women’s choices. Profiles featuring masculinized faces had approximately 56 percent lower odds of being accepted compared to profiles with feminized faces. However, the biographic text yielded unexpected results. Instead of favoring honest profiles, women showed a preference for the exaggerated text. Profiles with untrustworthy biographies had about 24 percent higher odds of acceptance compared to those with straightforward, trustworthy biographies.
“We were also surprised that profiles containing our ‘untrustworthy’ biographies were accepted more often than profiles containing the ‘trustworthy’ biographies,” Welling said. “The manipulation successfully changed perceptions of trustworthiness in the intended direction, so the finding suggests that participants may have been responding to other characteristics conveyed by those biographies, rather than simply preferring less trustworthy partners. We think it might have been something like perceived confidence in the untrustworthy bios because they tended to be more boastful.”
A woman’s level of religious belief also played a role in her swiping behavior, but not in the direction the researchers originally predicted. Higher religiosity predicted higher overall profile acceptance across the board. For each one-unit increase on the study’s seven-point religiosity scale, the odds of a profile being accepted increased by roughly 38 percent.
“The main takeaway is that religiosity was associated with greater initial receptivity to potential partners in our simulated online-dating task, rather than greater selectivity, which is the opposite of what we originally predicted,” Welling noted.
She cautioned that while the association was statistically reliable, it was not necessarily a massive shift in real-world behavior. “An odds ratio is not the same thing as saying that someone was 30% or 38% more likely to date someone,” Welling clarified. “The outcome in our study was simply whether a participant accepted a profile in a controlled, simulated swiping task. In other words, our findings suggest that religious women are more likely to be open to dating men with a greater range of characteristics, but not that they necessarily would accept more men after that initial swipe.”
In exploratory analyses, the researchers looked at why the women used dating apps in the first place. Women who used the apps with the goal of finding a relationship accepted fewer profiles overall, showing a 38 percent reduction in acceptance odds for each one-unit increase in relational motivation. Entertainment or exploratory motives for using the app had no statistical effect on acceptance rates.
The preference for exaggerated biographies is in tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2016, which found that dating profiles featuring heavy bragging reduced viewers’ intentions to contact the owner. This difference might be explained by how the new study was designed, as the simulated Tinder task measured immediate profile acceptance during rapid swiping rather than a deliberate intention to date the profile owner.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The simulated paradigm was not a fully interactive dating application, meaning real-world swiping behavior might differ. The acceptance of a profile in this specific task might reflect a general openness to new experiences or basic social interaction, rather than true romantic intent.
“The biggest caveat is that accepting a dating profile is not the same thing as choosing a partner, having sex with someone, entering a relationship, or taking a real-world interpersonal risk,” Welling emphasized. “Our measure captured an early-stage decision about whether a profile was sufficiently appealing to remain in consideration for potential further contact.”
She also warned against misinterpreting the biography finding as evidence that women prefer dishonest men. “Our biographies combined different aspects of self-presentation, including the extent to which information could theoretically be externally verified and the degree of selective self-presentation,” Welling explained. “Although they produced the intended differences in perceived trustworthiness, they may also have conveyed other characteristics, such as confidence… or like social status, that then influenced profile acceptance.”
The religiosity measure used in the study combined social elements, like attending religious services, with intrinsic elements, like personal beliefs. Social religiosity is often linked to higher interpersonal trust, which might explain the unexpectedly high acceptance rates among religious women. The study sample was also limited to young college-aged women in the United States, meaning the results might not automatically apply to other demographics.
Future research could use eye-tracking technology to see exactly which parts of a dating profile women pay the most attention to. Researchers might also separate different types of religious belief to better understand how they affect romantic risk-taking online. This would provide a better picture of how individuals navigate trust and uncertainty in the digital dating world.
“A major next step is to make the dating environment more realistic and to see how these findings translate into the in-person dating world,” Welling told PsyPost. “Our task captured the rapid decision-making aspect of swipe-based dating similar to dating apps like Tinder, but it was still a controlled simulation and results from face-to-face dating may differ.”
“I think the broader point is that online dating is an interesting setting for studying human decision-making because it makes the initial stages of mate evaluation unusually visible,” Welling concluded. “People are making rapid judgments from photographs, short biographies, and other limited cues, and those judgments reflect both characteristics of the profile and characteristics of the person doing the judging. Our findings suggest that we should be cautious about assuming that a characteristic associated with one aspect of mating psychology will necessarily predict behavior in another context.”
The study, “Holy swipes: the influence of religiosity on mate choice in online dating,” was authored by Katherine L. Sheetz and Lisa L. M. Welling.

UPWARD RELAUNCHES AS THE HOME OF MODERN COURTSHIP
With 72% of Gen Z wanting to get married,



Launched in 2020, Upward was built from a community that had strong conviction around faith, family and marriage. The relaunch builds on that foundation to welcome a broader generation reclaiming traditional courtship for modern life, where wanting a family is an ambition to embrace, not something to downplay.
"For a generation told to keep things casual and see where they go, saying you want marriage can almost feel countercultural," said

The relaunch brings modern courtship to life through a refreshed app experience designed to make values, future goals and relationship expectations more visible earlier in dating.
- Chivalry Mode is an opt-in experience for members who prefer a more traditional first-move dynamic. When both members opt in, he is encouraged to send the first message and she chooses whether to respond or politely unmatch.
- Marriage Timeline lets members share when they hope to get married and see whether potential matches share a similar timeline.
- Core Values gives members a way to show what matters most to them and quickly see whether they share a potential match's priorities.
This is modern courtship in action: women are clear about their standards, men pursue with purpose, and both move toward marriage together.
The clearest proof of Upward's purpose is why members join and why they leave. Nearly every Upward member ages 18–30 surveyed says they want a family, making "family" the platform's most-selected Core Value. And the #1 reason members say they leave is the outcome Upward is built for: they found someone worth leaving the app for.
The relaunch also introduces a new visual identity created in partnership with Corner Table Creative. A refined logo and app icon, distinctive typography and romantic imagery give Upward a bolder, more confident expression of its marriage-minded purpose. Drawing from Americana and the intimacy of a personal scrapbook, the new identity feels warm, nostalgic and distinctly human, anchored by subtle ring-inspired detail.
The accompanying "Wanted for Life" campaign brings that purpose to life through a playful, modern take on wanted posters. It celebrates the qualities members want in a lifelong partner, from good manners and meaningful effort to commitment that goes the distance. Through playful lines like "Known to change a tire, not his feelings for you" and "Often described as wifey material," Upward puts commitment and courtship where its members believe they belong: at the center of dating, not in a conversation saved for later.
"We wanted Upward's new brand to feel as intentional as the people who use it," said
The campaign will roll out across paid and organic social, streaming video and audio ads, with additional creative featuring real Upward couples who found lasting love on the app, bringing modern courtship to life from first match to marriage.

My dating app experiences haven’t been great. There have been ghosters and time-wasters and people who seemed fun over text but couldn’t hold a conversation in person.
My friends, though, have had some real Hinge horror stories.
One went on a date with a guy who told her he was planning to write his PhD thesis on “the philosophy of woman” but somehow didn’t notice that he had been explaining it for 30 minutes without letting the woman across from him speak.
Another girl went on a date with someone who made her do their laundry, and pay for it. They claimed they had a new debit card that didn’t work and hadn’t been able to do their laundry for two weeks as a result.
And one friend experienced “Hinge-cest”, where she and all her friends had ended up dating the same men. There are “Hinge celebrities” who have gone on so many dates that their reputation precedes them.
Sounds like the ideal environment for meeting the love of your life, right?
Despite the technology’s poor reputation, it feels like everyone my age is on the apps. However, I only know a handful who have actually ended up in relationships with people they met online. Most, after weeks or months of scrolling, texting and going on dates, become frustrated and delete the app. And then, after failing to meet someone in real life, they re-download it.
So why are so many young people using dating apps if they don’t work? I believe it’s because my generation doesn’t know how to date in person.
Gen Z spent some of its formative dating and socialising years in lockdown, and we’ve grown up communicating over the internet. So it makes sense that this has had a lingering effect.
Dating apps seem to offer an easy way out. I do find it easier to speak to a new person online; shyness and awkwardness don’t come across over text. And perhaps most importantly, online rejection is far less humiliating.
But our dependence on dating apps might be making dating harder for us.
The idea that everyone is on Hinge has made making a move in person a completely foreign idea. Gen Z has lost the willingness to take a chance and just ask someone out, which dating has always relied on.
The gamification of dating makes us view it as a lazy activity – something we can do without leaving our bedrooms.
What’s worse is the horrible culture fostered by these apps. Ghosting people and talking to more than 10 people at once are considered normal. It’s no wonder users seem to forget they’re interacting with real humans. Similarly, your entire judgment of someone is based on a few photos.
None of this is conducive to genuine connection. It’s a tick-box model of dating, where you reject anyone who doesn’t fit your “ideal partner” criteria based on their photo and a few titbits of information. All this does is teach us to how to market ourselves to please other people and relentlessly judge others.
Dating in real life can be the opposite: you might end up with someone who doesn’t tick all the boxes you thought you wanted, but who ticks others that you didn’t realise you needed. The most important things, like real-life chemistry, communication style and personality, can’t be captured in a dating-app profile.
Although dating apps can have value for those who don’t have many opportunities to meet new people in real life, we need to break away from the mindset that they’re the only way to connect.
After the end of my last relationship, a friend told me to “keep going out, meeting new people, and something would happen eventually”. So, I made a conscious effort to say yes to every invitation that came my way – whether it was a spontaneous dinner, a side-quest that sends the night in a new direction, or a new book club. Even when I felt busy, or tired, or didn’t think I’d enjoy it.
And my life has become so much richer as a result. I’m meeting interesting people every day, going to places I haven’t been before, and trying out new things. Last week I spent an evening at a small art gallery in Brunswick, another at a themed house party, and a morning at a philosophy reading group. I’m much happier than I was when I was scrolling Hinge. And I know something will happen when it’s meant to.
I’m learning that dating in a meaningful way takes courage, patience and rejection – like it did for generations before mine. In any case, I think I’d still rather be rejected in real life than do an internet stranger’s washing on a first date.
Saria Ratnam is a University of Melbourne arts student.

item.content:encoded:
If you’re looking for a serious relationship, dating apps can start to feel like a particularly exhausting game of “What the hell are you actually looking for?” Sure, their profile says “long-term relationship,” but does that mean marriage? A committed partner? Someone to split a Costco membership with? Or someone who will text you “wyd” every Thursday night for the next six months?
The good news is that people absolutely do use dating apps to find real, long-term relationships. And while certain apps are designed to make finding a serious partner easier, there’s no single app that magically contains all the people ready to commit. “Any dating app or website can be good for long-term relationships if you are honest and intentional about what you want from the beginning,” says Rachel Needle, PsyD, a licensed psychologist and co-director of Modern Sex Therapy Institutes.
Still, choosing an app that attracts people looking for the same kind of relationship you are can save you a whole lot of time. Just as important is making your own intentions clear. Clinical sexologist Tatyannah King, MSW, recommends explicitly stating that you’re looking for something long-term in your profile, even if doing so means getting fewer matches. She also suggests including specific details that actually tell people something about your life and personality. Basically, you’re trying to find someone compatible, not collect every available human within a 15-mile radius.
Ready to get back out there? Below, we’re breaking down the best dating apps for serious relationships, who they’re best for, what they cost, and what you should know before downloading.
1. Bumble
Best For:
Women who want more control over how conversations start.
Why We Picked It:
“Bumble is an ideal app for people who are looking for long-term partnerships, especially for women who date men,” King says. “As someone who dates with intention and prefers long-term relationships over short flings, I’ve personally also found it helpful to pay for the premium version. I noticed that men who are paying for the premium version of Bumble’s dating app seem to be more intentional about dating.”
She also loves Bumble’s Opening Moves feature, which lets women set prompts that their matches can respond to, giving them another way to get a conversation going beyond sending the first message themselves. Matches expire if no one sends a message within 24 hours, which can help keep things moving instead of letting a promising match sit untouched for three weeks.
Who It’s For:
Bumble is open to daters of all genders and orientations. In heterosexual matches, women traditionally initiate the conversation, but Opening Moves gives them the option to set a prompt that a match can respond to instead. In same-gender and nonbinary connections, either person can start the conversation.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
Pros:
- Opening Moves gives women more flexibility over how conversations get started
- Snooze Mode lets you temporarily hide your profile when you need a dating-app break
- Plenty of prompts and profile features to help show off your personality
- SuperSwipes let you signal extra interest in a potential match
- Incognito Mode lets Premium and Premium+ members only be seen by people they’ve already liked
- Paid subscriptions offer perks like unlimited likes and advanced filters
- Travel Mode lets Premium and Premium+ members change their location before or during a trip
Cons:
- The 24-hour window to start a conversation can feel limiting if you don’t check the app regularly
- Some of the most useful features, including Incognito and Travel Mode, require a paid subscription
- Bumble’s conversation rules can take a minute to get used to if you’re coming from apps where anyone can immediately message a match
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Bumble Boost starts at around $14.99 per week
- Bumble Premium starts at around $27.99 per week
- Bumble Premium+ starts at around $39.99 per week
2. Hinge
Best For:
Daters who want to know more than someone’s height and favorite vacation spot before matching.
Why We Picked It:
The self-proclaimed “dating app designed to be deleted,” Hinge is an obvious contender if your ultimate goal is to get off dating apps altogether. “If you're searching for a dating platform that prioritizes depth over quick swipes, Hinge might be just what you're looking for,” says Mariah Freya, sex education expert and founder of Beducated. “It combines the best of Tinder's ease of use with Match's focus on genuine connections.”
Profiles include photos and videos, answers to prompts, and details like dating intentions and relationship type, giving you plenty to work with when deciding whether you might actually like someone. You can also like or comment on a specific part of someone’s profile rather than simply swiping on the whole person, and Hinge’s newer Convo Starters feature offers personalized suggestions based on a match’s profile when your brain simply cannot come up with another opening line.
Who It’s For:
Hinge is open to daters of all genders and orientations, but it’s particularly useful if you want more information about potential matches upfront and are looking for something beyond a hookup.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
Pros:
- Detailed profiles include photos, videos, voice, prompts, dating intentions, and relationship preferences
- You can like or comment on specific parts of someone’s profile, giving you a built-in conversation starter
- Convo Starters can help when you have absolutely no idea what to say
- Selfie Verification can help confirm that matches look like the person in their profile
- Hinge’s We Met feature asks about your dates after you exchange phone numbers with a match and uses that feedback to improve future recommendations
- Hinge+ offers unlimited likes and lets you see everyone who has liked you
- HingeX adds features like enhanced recommendations and Priority Likes
Cons:
- Free users have a limited number of likes
- Some of the features that make Hinge significantly easier to use are behind paid subscriptions
- Detailed profiles are great if you want depth, less great if filling out dating-app prompts is your personal hell
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Hinge+ starts at around $29.99 per month
- HingeX starts at around $49.99 per month
3. Tinder
Best For:
Having a ton of options.
Why We Picked It:
Tinder is basically the reason swiping became synonymous with dating apps in the first place, and its sheer size is still one of its biggest selling points. The app is available in more than 190 countries and has racked up more than 55 billion matches, so if your biggest dating problem is simply finding enough people to date, Tinder certainly gives you options. And while it has a reputation as a hookup app, you can specify what you’re looking for with Relationship Goals, including a long-term partner.
Who It’s For:
Tinder is open to daters of all genders and orientations and is a particularly good option if you want a large dating pool. Because people use Tinder for everything from casual hookups to serious relationships, though, pay attention to Relationship Goals and be upfront about what you’re looking for if long-term love is the goal.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop via Tinder for Web
Pros:
- Huge dating pool with users around the world
- Easy to set up and start swiping
- Relationship Goals help you communicate what you’re looking for
- Photo Verification lets users verify that they look like their profile photos
- Rewind lets subscribers undo their last Like or Nope
- Passport Mode lets you change your location and match with people elsewhere
- Tinder Platinum includes Priority Likes, which helps your Likes and Super Likes get seen faster
Cons:
- A huge dating pool also means more profiles to wade through
- People use Tinder for all kinds of connections, so not everyone you encounter will be looking for a serious relationship
- Free users don’t get unlimited Likes
- Features like Rewind and Passport require a subscription or separate purchase
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Tinder Plus starts at around $9.99 per month
- Tinder Gold starts at around $13.99 per month
4. Hily
Best For:
Gen Z daters looking for a more intentional, inclusive dating experience.
Why We Picked It:
With a large Gen Z user base, Hily is clearly geared toward younger daters. The app has more than 43 million downloads and puts a big emphasis on authenticity, compatibility, and helping users find people who are actually looking for the same things they are.
One feature that especially stands out is Consent Guard, which is designed to help prevent unsolicited explicit messages and images. If the technology detects potentially sexual content, it prompts the sender to ask for consent before sending it, giving the recipient the option to accept or decline. Because nothing kills the possibility of a meaningful connection quite like an unsolicited nude from someone you exchanged three messages with.
Who It’s For:
Hily is especially suited to Gen Z daters who want to meet people based on more than a few carefully curated photos. It may also appeal to anyone who appreciates extra control over the kinds of sexual messages or images they receive while dating online.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
Pros:
- Particularly geared toward Gen Z and younger daters
- Consent Guard helps prevent unsolicited explicit messages and photos from reaching you without your consent
- Discover offers another way to find potential matches based on your interests and dating intentions
- Profile verification and other safety features help screen potential matches
- Compatibility features offer another way to evaluate potential matches beyond their photos
- You can add music to your profile, because music compatibility is very much a thing
Cons:
- Some features require a paid subscription
- May appeal less to older daters looking for a more traditional dating-app experience
Price:
- Free to download and use
- Hily Premium starts at around $14.99 per week
- Hily Premium+ starts at around $24.99 per week
- Additional in-app purchases, including profile boosts, are available
5. eharmony
Best For:
Daters who are serious about finding a long-term partner.
Why We Picked It:
eharmony has been around since 2000, which is approximately 400 years in dating-app time, but its focus on long-term compatibility is also what keeps it relevant for people who are serious about finding a relationship. Instead of immediately throwing you into an endless stack of profiles, the app has you complete a detailed Compatibility Quiz and uses your answers to generate matches and compatibility information.
“If you're ready to say ‘I do,’ then eharmony is there to guide you along the way,” Freya says. “Renowned for its emphasis on long-term commitment, it's like the Charlotte York of dating apps—traditional and mostly geared towards heterosexual relationships.” While you certainly don’t need to be ready for marriage tomorrow to use it, the more involved setup process and detailed profiles may appeal to daters who are willing to put a little more time into finding a compatible partner.
Who It’s For:
People looking for a serious, long-term relationship who don’t mind spending more time setting up their profile and answering compatibility questions upfront. It may also appeal to daters who prefer a more structured matching process over simply swiping through profiles.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop
Pros:
- Detailed profiles and an in-depth Compatibility Quiz
- Compatibility information can help you evaluate potential matches
- Matching process is designed around long-term compatibility
- Particularly geared toward relationship-minded daters
- Free Basic membership lets you create a profile and browse matches
Cons:
- More time-consuming to set up than swipe-first apps
- Unlimited messaging and several other features require Premium
- Premium subscriptions require a longer commitment than many competing apps
- May feel a little traditional compared with newer dating apps
Price:
- Free Basic membership available
- Premium Light, typically a six-month commitment, runs roughly $59 to $69 per month
- Premium Plus, typically a 12-month commitment, runs roughly $38 to $50 per month
- Premium Extra, typically a 24-month commitment, runs roughly $29 to $33 per month
6. Match
Best For:
Serious daters who want a large, established dating pool.
Why We Picked It:
Match has been around since 1995, making it one of the OG online dating platforms—and there’s something to be said for an app that has survived approximately every era of internet dating. Unlike platforms that lean heavily into casual swiping, Match has long positioned itself toward people looking for relationships.
“Match is my top choice for its ability to cater to individuals in their 30s and 40s seeking meaningful connections,” Freya says. “Its large user base offers a wide range of like-minded adults looking for genuine relationships.” Profiles also give you plenty of space to spell out who you are and what you’re looking for, which can be especially useful when the goal is finding someone you might actually want to date long-term.
Who It’s For:
Relationship-minded daters who want a more traditional online dating experience and plenty of information about potential matches before deciding whether to connect.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop
Pros:
- Large, established dating pool
- Detailed profiles let you learn more about potential matches upfront
- Geared toward people looking for relationships
- Search and filtering options can help narrow down potential matches
Cons:
- Many features require a paid subscription
- Can feel more traditional than newer dating apps
- Paid memberships can get pricey
- Longer subscriptions are generally billed upfront rather than month-to-month
Price:
- Free to join and use with limited features
- Standard plans run roughly $34.45 per month for three months, $24.48 per month for six months, or $21.84 per month for 12 months
- Premium plans run roughly $40.41 per month for three months, $26.51 per month for six months, or $23.11 per month for 12 months
- Multi-month plans are generally charged in full at the beginning of the subscription
7. OkCupid
Best For:
Daters who want to get specific about compatibility.
Why We Picked It:
OkCupid has been around since 2004, but it’s managed to evolve beyond its early-internet-dating roots. One of its biggest draws is the sheer number of questions you can answer about everything from relationships and lifestyle to politics, sex, and approximately whatever else you might want to know about someone before agreeing to spend two hours across a table from them.
Your answers help determine your compatibility with potential matches, and you can also specify what kind of relationship you’re looking for. That makes OkCupid especially useful if you have particular values, preferences, or dealbreakers you’d rather get out of the way sooner rather than later.
Who It’s For:
Daters who want a more inclusive app and like having plenty of information about potential matches upfront. It’s also a good option if you’d rather use compatibility questions to narrow down your dating pool than rely primarily on photos and a few prompts.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS and Android
- Available on desktop
Pros:
- Lots of compatibility questions to help you find people with similar values and preferences
- Inclusive gender and sexual-orientation options
- You can specify the type of relationship you’re looking for
- Free version offers plenty of functionality
- Available on desktop as well as mobile
Cons:
- Answering enough questions to get the most out of the compatibility features takes some time
- Some features and filters require a paid subscription
- The amount of information can feel like a lot if you prefer a simpler swipe-and-go experience
Price:
- Free to download and use
- OkCupid Premium starts at around $19.99 per month
- Additional paid features and Boosts are available
8. Flure
Best For:
Sex-positive daters looking for less traditional dating-app rules.
Why We Picked It:
A serious relationship doesn’t necessarily have to follow the traditional dating-app playbook, which is where Flure comes in. The app takes a more open-ended approach to dating, encouraging users to meet people and see where the connection goes rather than requiring them to define exactly what they’re looking for upfront. It also puts a particular emphasis on sex positivity, inclusivity, and creating a space where users can be open about what they want.
Flure also puts an emphasis on safety and communication. Its in-app features include Safe Mode, which helps protect users from unsolicited explicit content, and Flure Sparks, a game designed to help matches get to know each other and talk about everything from everyday interests to sex and relationships.
Who It’s For:
Sex-positive and open-minded daters who prefer a less rigid approach to defining what they’re looking for and want an app that leaves room for different kinds of connections.
Platform Info:
- Available on iOS

item.dc:creator: Clare Armstrong
item.description: In short: Almost all women surveyed in a new Australian study reported encountering harmful behaviour on dating apps, with many taking their own precautions to stay safe. Researchers say platforms should do more to prevent systemic risks as the federal government considers a digital duty of care. What's next?
